3. It is stated in the plaint that Abdur Rahim was original owner of the suit land, by kabala executed on 1l-5-1982 and registered on 11-5-1982 transferred the suit land to Shahazuddin Mollah and others. Shahazuddin Mollah and his wife after purchase was in possession, thereafter sold the suit land to Md. Miazuddin and to his wife, Mosammat Safia Akhtar alias Sapia by registered kabala executed on 13-8-1995 and registered on 14-8-1995, who, in turn sold the suit land to the plaintiffs by kabala No.9846 dated 14-8-1995. It is stated in the plaint that this land having been situated at the side of Sadar Road, plaintiffs resides 200/250 yards from this purchased land and thereafter, made development in the case land by expending Tk. 2,00,000. In the suit land, plaintiffs constructed a two storied building, which, in total consists of 32 rooms with 9 toilets. Out of the aforesaid rooms, in 3 rooms plaintiffs installed shops which have been managed by his only son. Plaintiffs also constructed ground safety tank. Plaintiffs got notice of pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.1 of 1996, appeared and contested the case in which plaintiffs lost up to the Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court. Thereafter, while preemptor went for possession plaintiffs instituted the suit, on the ground that as per section 6 of the Land Reforms Ordinance, 1984 plaintiffs cannot be evict from the suit property 

 “5. It appears from the submission of the learned Advocates of both the parties that written statement in the suit has already been filed by the defendant and the question of maintainability of the suit has clearly been raised in the said written statement. None of the learned Advocates could appraise the court whether any issue regarding maintain- ability of the suit has been framed or not. But from the written objection it does not appear that such question of maintainability was raised before the trial court at the time of hearing of the injunction matter. It does not appear from the impugned order that any such question was raised before the court below at the time of hearing the temporary injection matter. Court is not required to look into maintainability of the suit at the time of hearing of the injunction matter. Maintainability of the suit is to be decided after filing of the written statement and framing of any issue on such point. So I do not find any merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the suit is not justified in allowing the prayer for temporary injunction. The mistake pointed out by the learned Advocate for the appellant can be corrected at any stage of the suit by amending the cause title of the plaint. So it will not be proper to make any finding on the said question at the stage of the hearing interlocutory injunction matter as the matter was not raised before the court below depriving the plaintiff opportunity to meet such objection." 

 "6. No eviction, etc, from the homestead Any land used as a homestead by its owner in the rural area shall be exempted from all legal processes, including seizure, distress, attachment or sale by any office, court or any other authority and the owner of such land shall not be divested or dispossessed of the land or evicted there from by any means: Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to the acquisition of such homestead under any law." 

 12. I have examined the written objection filed by the purchaser opposite party No.1 in the trial court carefully. In this written objection the purchaser nowhere has stated that he has been using the case land as his home- stead. Though in this written objection purchaser opposite party No.1 has stated that after purchasing the case land he has constructed one pucca hut and a boundary wall on the case land by spending a total amount of Taka 1,28,885.79 and has been possessing the same but he has not stated that he has been residing there i.e. in that hut. In the deposition of purchaser-opposite party No.1 also there is nothing to the effect that he has been possessing the case land as his homestead. Rather, during cross-examination, this opposite party No.1 has stated that he has got his paternal homestead which consists of 4 rooms and which is 3 kilometre off from the case land. Save and except the opposite party No.1 himself no other man has been examined from his side. It should be mentioned here that this purchaser opposite party No. J neither in his written objection nor in his deposition has stated any such case that the case land is not agricultural land and as such this case for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not maintain- able. Rather, in his written objection the purchaser opposite party No. 1 has stated that he has constructed one hut within the case land and has been possessing the remaining of the case land through cultivation. However, both the courts below appear to have relied on some statements of the PW 1. This PW 1, during cross-examination, has stated that the opposite party No. 1 has one shop hut, a tube-well and a boundary wall within the case land and that after filing of this case for pre-emption the opposite party No. 1 constructed those structures on the case land. However, this PW 1 did not state at all that the purchaser opposite party No. 1 has been using the case land as his homestead. So I find that there was no evidence at all before the learned courts below to hold that the purchaser-opposite party No. 1 has been using the case land as his homestead. The mere fact that the purchaser constructed some structures within the case land after his purchase does not attract section 6 of Land Reforms Ordinance 1984 to invalidate a pre-emption proceeding under section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It appears that in view of the above referred statements of the PW 1 the learned appellate court has further observed that the case land is not agricultural land and, as such, this case for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not maintainable. This observation of the learned appellate court also is erroneous. Because, admittedly, the structure on the case land was constructed after the impugned sale. There is no evidence at all on record to show that at the time of impugned sale the case land was not agricultural land. Rather the own statement of the purchaser-opposite party No.1 in his written objection to the effect the has been possessing the remaining portion of the case land through cultivation proves that at the time of his purchase the case land was agricultural land. The subsequent construction of any shop or other structure within the case land does not invalidate this case for preemption filed under section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act." 

 15. It has been decided by the various authority of Apex Court of the Country that plaint is to be rejected within 4 comers of the plaint and in rejection of the plaint defendant's materials should not be relied. Learned Judge as it appears held that in the plaint it has been stated that in the pre-emption proceeding plaintiffs lost up to Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court as such he has no title to invoke section 6 of the Land Reform Ordinance, 1984. In the Apex Court of the Hon'ble Supreme Court it is held that legal proceeding under section 6 of the Land Reform Ordinance, 1984 available to a person who is owner of the property and the property is at rural area. Here we may refer to law itself i.e. Land Reform Ordinance, 1984. Section 2 of the Land Reform Ordinance, 1984 speaks bargadar is protected by section 6 of the Land Reform Ordinance and Bargadar means a person who under the system generally known as adhi, barga or bhag cultivate the land of another person on condition of delivering a share of produce of such land to that person. And homestead has been defined as a dwelling house with out-house, tanks and enclosures immediately connected with it covering an area of not more than one standard bigha. Then 'malik' has been defined a person or an organization, body or authority holding agricultural land. Owner has been defined as in relation to a barga land, means the person from whom the bargadar gets the land for cultivation under a barga contract. These persons are protected under section 6 of the Land Reform Ordinance, 1984.
